newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Hurricane Lili lashes Bahamas, heads to Bermuda.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Lili lashes Bahamas, heads to Bermuda.

text.p: Hurricane Lili headed toward Bermuda on Saturday after rampaging through the Bahamas where it ripped off roofs and brought down telegraph poles on San Salvador, but left no reported casualties,

Lili, which slammed Cuba on Friday without claiming lives, pounded the island of San Salvador in the early hours of Saturday. Winston Bonaby, chief councilor in the local government, said San Salvador had been devastated.
"The island has been battered, very few houses remain untouched. Fortunately there were no injuries and no loss of life," he told Reuters, adding it was the worst storm in 14 years.
The National Hurricane Center in Miami said people in Bermuda were told to closely monitor Lili's progress.
Lili's center was located near latitude 26.0 north and longitude 70.3 west or about 550 miles (890 km) southwest of Bermuda at 5 p.m EDT (2100 GMT), forecasters said.

It was moving east northeast at 28 mph (44 kph) and was expected to plow on in the same direction for the next 24 hours. Maximum sustained winds were near 115 mph (185 kph) and some weakening was likely on Sunday, they said.
Hurricane force winds extended up to 85 miles (140 km) from its center.
The storm cut a swathe across several Bahamian islands before hitting San Salvador. Roofs were ripped off houses, trees and communication poles were felled and land flooded in the capital Nassau.
Elbert Thompson, a reporter at the Bahamas Broadcasting Corporation, said tropical storm stength winds lashed Nassau and the island of south Andros.
"The eye of the hurricane went right over Georgetown (Great Exuma) and caused extensive damage," he said.
Thompson said no loss of life was reported and the only casualties were minor injuries from broken glass.
The storm also surged through Long Island and over Rum Cay and onto Cat Island where crops were badly damaged.

It then descended on San Salvador where the airport control tower was toppled onto the runway. In the port of Cockburn Town, home to most of the island's 700 residents, roofs and balconies were torn off.
Palm trees were snapped and driftwood and debris were strewn across beaches.
At the island's Club Med resort, angry tourists complained they received little advice about how to cope with a hurricane.
Clem Cleri, 46, from Chino Hills, California, said: "A lot of people were scared and I don't think they gave out enough information."
About 260 vacationers, mostly Germans, Americans and French, were booked into the resort. Club Med spokeswoman Margo Leader said no one was injured.
Schools had closed early on Friday in the Bahamas, an archipelego of hundreds of islands stretching more than 600 miles (950 km) in the Atlantic.
San Salvador, a 25-mile long (40 km) island, claims to be the first place in the New World where explorer Christopher Columbus set foot in 1492.
Flooding from the storm was blamed for 10 deaths in Nicaragua, Honduras and Costa Rica earlier in the week but there were no reports of deaths in Cuba, officials said.
Cuban authorities said on Saturday the storm caused widespread damage to crops including citrus fruits and bananas and about 7,000 homes were damaged.
